one_liner: Tiny self-hosting C compiler/JIT that compiles about 9x faster than gcc -O0, trading away optimization.
what_it_does: TinyCC (tcc) is a complete, self-hosting ANSI C compiler, assembler and linker bundled into one roughly 100KB binary, targeting ISO C99 plus many C11 features and GNU extensions including inline asm. It works both as a gcc-compatible command-line compiler and, via the libtcc library, as an embeddable in-memory JIT: compile a C string or file with tcc_compile_string()/tcc_add_file() and then run it with tcc_run() or relocate it and pull out symbols with tcc_get_symbol(). It also supports 'C scripting': adding a '#!/usr/local/bin/tcc -run' shebang lets a .c file execute directly like a shell script, no separate build step.
how_it_is_fast: It skips almost everything gcc's pipeline does beyond translation: no real optimizer (tcc has no flag comparable to -O1/-O2/-O3), a single fast pass from source straight to machine code, and its own integrated preprocessor/assembler/linker avoid forking out to separate cc1/as/ld processes. It also natively supports 6 target architectures (i386, x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V64, plus legacy TMS320C67xx) with a simple, non-SSA-optimizing code generator per target. The cost of skipping optimization is codegen roughly at gcc -O0/-O1 quality.
when_to_use: Tight edit-compile-run development loops where compiler latency, not runtime speed, dominates iteration time
Ad hoc 'C scripting' -- running a .c file directly via a #!tcc -run shebang instead of compiling a real binary
Embedding a C compiler/JIT inside another program (via libtcc) for runtime code generation, e.g. compiling small C snippets to native code and calling them in-process
Bootstrapping or rescue environments where binary size matters (GNU Mes uses tcc to bootstrap a build from source)
Local/CI dev builds of large C codebases where a project bundles tcc for fast iteration and uses a real compiler for release builds (this is how the V language uses it)
when_not_to_use: Producing optimized release binaries -- there is no optimization pass comparable to gcc -O1/-O2/-O3, so generated code is measurably slower
Code relying on full C11 or the broader GNU C extension surface -- tcc covers 'many' C11 features and GNU extensions, not all of them (not documented as 100% coverage)
C++ code -- tcc is a C compiler only
Toolchains that depend on gcc/clang-specific features such as LTO, sanitizers, or vendor-specific builtins not implemented by tcc
Programs combining the -b bounds checker with signal handlers or fork() in a multi-threaded process -- the docs call this out as a known incompatibility because the bounds-checking code uses locks

integration.form: source-drop / standalone compiler binary (CLI, gcc-like flags); optional static and shared libtcc library for embedding as an in-memory JIT
integration.dependencies: none required to build (self-hosting: ./configure && make, or make test); optional -lpthread when using the -pthread flag
integration.min_toolchain: Any ANSI C (C89) host compiler to bootstrap from source, or tcc itself; as a language target it implements ISO C99, many ISO C11 features, and GNU C extensions (inline asm, _Thread_local, __attribute__((cleanup)), _Static_assert, asm goto, stdatomic)
integration.platforms: x86 (i386), x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V64, legacy TMS320C67xx; Linux/BSD (ELF), native macOS x86-64 (Mach-O), Windows (PE, see tcc-win32.txt), Android (position-independent executables)
integration.thread_safety: Not a single shared global state: separate TCCState compilation contexts can be created and used concurrently from different threads (see tests/libtcc_test_mt.c in the repo). Per-state concurrent use from multiple threads simultaneously is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- tcc accepts many gcc-compatible command-line flags and is used as a gcc substitute in several build systems (V language dev builds, GNU Mes bootstrap), but incomplete C11/GNU-extension coverage, no LTO/sanitizers, and gcc -O0/-O1-level codegen mean it cannot replace gcc for anything needing full standards coverage or optimized output

gotchas: The -b bounds checker is incompatible with signal handlers (checking is disabled inside them) and interacts badly with fork() in multi-threaded programs, per tcc-doc.texi -- both stem from locking inside the bounds-checking runtime
Bound-checked code (-b) is not included in shared libraries; the main executable must itself be built with -b for the checker to take effect
Codegen quality sits around gcc -O0/-O1; don't compare tcc binaries' runtime speed to an optimized gcc/clang build
-std=version only distinguishes c11/gnu11 (sets __STDC_VERSION__ to 201112) from everything else (199901); it isn't a fine-grained standards switch like gcc's
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tcc over zapcc or MIR/c2m when you want a mature, widely-deployed, general-purpose C compiler and embeddable JIT rather than a narrower research/prototype tool: zapcc is an abandoned Clang fork focused on incremental C++ template caching, and MIR/c2m is a newer, more experimental C-to-MIR JIT (bigger claimed speedup, less production track record). Neither zapcc nor cg_clif target C the way tcc does (zapcc is C++-only via Clang, cg_clif is a Rust backend), so for straight C dev-loop speed or in-process C JITing, tcc is the direct fit.
verified_claims_summary: On Fabrice Bellard's own tcc benchmark page, compiling the Links web browser (76,936 source lines, but 1,950,947 lines / 67.2MB actually compiled due to repeated header inclusion) on a 2.4GHz Pentium 4: TinyCC 0.9.22 finished in 2.27s (859,000 lines/s, 29.6MB/s) versus GCC 3.2 at -O0 in 20.0s (98,000 lines/s, 3.4MB/s), about a 9x wall-clock advantage. Both compilers ran with no comparable optimization flags enabled (tcc has none), and the hardware/compiler versions are roughly 2003-2005 era.
